performers: Barbara Schubert, the DuPage Symphony Orchestra
intro: After three movements of marching and dancing, an alto sings the Second Symphony’s first words. Urlicht is a small, stubborn prayer: even an angel cannot turn its traveller away from God.

sections.label: A · Alto and brass chorale
sections.mNote: One voice, answered by a hymn for brass

sections.label: B · The alto sings of suffering
sections.mNote: The vocal line climbs through chromatic harmony

cues.title: One voice, then brass
cues.text: An alto begins with three rising notes. Trumpets answer with a hymn, unfolding that small upward phrase into an arch. Mahler marks the song Sehr feierlich, aber schlicht — very solemn, yet simple.
cues.evidence: Mahler, Symphony No. 2, Hofmeister full score (1897), movement IV, pp. 128–129. Lew Smoley describes the three-note invocation and trumpet chorale: https://mahlerfoundation.org/mahler/listening-guide/listening-guide-movement-4-urlicht-sehr-feierlich-aber-schlicht/
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Suffering bends the tune
cues.text: The alto sings of human misery. Semitones creep into the vocal line and the harmony beneath it; the brass hymn’s plain steps become harder to climb. When the singer longs for heaven, the hymn returns.
cues.evidence: Smoley describes the chromatic setting of the second and third lines and the return to the chorale melody in the following lines: https://mahlerfoundation.org/mahler/listening-guide/listening-guide-movement-4-urlicht-sehr-feierlich-aber-schlicht/
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: A summer manuscript
cues.text: Steinbach am Attersee, 19 July 1893: Mahler dates an orchestral manuscript of Urlicht. He is also working on the Second Symphony’s dances that summer. The song already exists before he decides to give it this place in the symphony.
cues.evidence: The dated manuscript is Zweig MS 49, folio 6r. Mahler’s 1895 letter to Hermann Behn establishes that the song preceded the decision to include it: https://mahlerfoundation.org/mahler/compositions/symphony-no-2/symphony-no-2-movement-4-lied-1-urlicht-sehr-feierlich-aber-schlicht/

cues.title: The angel on the road
cues.text: The prayer becomes a story. In B♭ minor, a nimble clarinet tune accompanies the traveller’s encounter with an angel; a solo violin spins a longer melody as the harmony moves towards A major. The angel tries to send the traveller back.
cues.evidence: Smoley identifies the B♭-minor middle, clarinet tune, solo violin and move to A major. The encounter is in the Wunderhorn text: https://mahlerfoundation.org/mahler/listening-guide/listening-guide-movement-4-urlicht-sehr-feierlich-aber-schlicht/
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: The traveller stands firm
cues.text: The traveller refuses. The alto’s phrases climb again and again over trembling strings, each new chord lifting the reply higher. The poem’s speaker comes from God and insists on returning to God; the little prayer has acquired a fierce will.
cues.evidence: Hofmeister score, movement IV, pp. 131–133; Smoley describes the rising chromatic chords, string tremolo and ascending vocal sequences: https://mahlerfoundation.org/mahler/listening-guide/listening-guide-movement-4-urlicht-sehr-feierlich-aber-schlicht/
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Strings finish the sentence
cues.text: The singer stops before the harmony has come to rest. The strings complete the cadence in D♭ major, quietly carrying the prayer beyond its last word.
cues.evidence: Hofmeister score, movement IV, p. 133. Smoley identifies the orchestral cadence after the unfinished vocal phrase: https://mahlerfoundation.org/mahler/listening-guide/listening-guide-movement-4-urlicht-sehr-feierlich-aber-schlicht/
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

transitions.title: The alto resumes the prayer
transitions.to: B · The alto sings of suffering
transitions.how: The brass chorale settles in D♭ major. The alto resumes over strings, and the words about human suffering draw semitones into the melody. Mahler keeps the invocation’s upward reach while moving its plain hymn chords into more troubled harmony.
transitions.evidence: Hofmeister score, movement IV, pp. 128–130; Lew Smoley’s account of the chorale and chromatic vocal continuation: https://mahlerfoundation.org/mahler/listening-guide/listening-guide-movement-4-urlicht-sehr-feierlich-aber-schlicht/

transitions.title: An oboe turn, then clarinet
transitions.from: B · The alto sings of suffering
transitions.to: C · An angel bars the road
transitions.how: The alto leaves the cadence unfinished; an oboe completes it with a turning phrase. The middle section begins in B♭ minor. Clarinet figures spring up around the voice, and a solo violin extends them into a longer tune as the traveller tells of the angel.
transitions.evidence: Smoley describes the oboe’s cadential turn and the B♭-minor middle for alto, clarinet and solo violin: https://mahlerfoundation.org/mahler/listening-guide/listening-guide-movement-4-urlicht-sehr-feierlich-aber-schlicht/

transitions.title: The reply climbs through semitones
transitions.from: C · An angel bars the road
transitions.how: After the middle section’s excursion to A major, rising chromatic chords carry the alto’s refusal upwards. String tremolo runs beneath the voice. The ascending phrases recall the first stanza’s account of suffering; the final D♭-major cadence waits until after the singer has finished.
transitions.evidence: Hofmeister score, movement IV, pp. 131–133; Smoley on the A-major excursion, rising chords, tremolo and final string cadence: https://mahlerfoundation.org/mahler/listening-guide/listening-guide-movement-4-urlicht-sehr-feierlich-aber-schlicht/

source.title: Mahler, Symphony No. 2, IV. Urlicht, full score (Hofmeister; Universal Edition reprint)
source.locator: Fourth movement, pp. 128–133, rehearsal figures 1–6: alto prayer, brass chorale, clarinet and solo-violin middle, and the closing string cadence.

timeline.note: The alto begins above muted strings; the brass waits to answer with its chorale.
Trumpets and horns harmonise the chorale above bassoons, contrabassoon and the sustained bass.
The alto resumes over sustained string harmony after the brass chorale.
Soft trumpet recollections answer the alto while the string harmony moves beneath the phrase.
The alto’s rising phrase gives way to an oboe turn over sustained strings.
Clarinet and solo violin accompany the traveller’s story, with harp notes and a glockenspiel stroke.
Piccolo doubles the ornamented violin line; harps and soft strings surround the encounter with the angel.
The alto’s refusal rises over trembling strings, harp chords, soft horns and bassoons.
The vocal crest gathers wind and brass support before the slow closing phrase.
Quiet clarinets and bassoons colour the final vocal line; two harps spread the closing harmony.
Muted divided strings complete the D♭-major cadence after the alto’s last word.

composer.epithet: A conductor who composed in the summers, and wanted each symphony to hold a whole world — the sublime and the street band together.
facts: Vienna Conservatory, 1875–78: piano with Julius Epstein, composition with Franz Krenn; attended Bruckner’s university lectures
Budapest Royal Opera 1888–91 · Hamburg Stadttheater 1891–97 · Vienna Court Opera 1897–1907 · Metropolitan Opera and New York Philharmonic 1908–11
In summer huts at Steinbach am Attersee, Maiernigg on the Wörthersee, and Toblach in the Dolomites
Nine numbered symphonies and an unfinished Tenth; Das Lied von der Erde; orchestral songs

quote.text: The symphony must be like the world. It must embrace everything.
quote.source: To Jean Sibelius, Helsinki, 1907, as Sibelius remembered it

composer.background:
Mahler was born in a Bohemian village and grew up in the garrison town of Iglau (Jihlava), the second of fourteen children, eight of whom died young. Iglau gave him the sounds that never left his music: bugle calls and marches from the barracks, Czech and German folk song, the town band, the synagogue and the Catholic church. A story he told late in life, to Sigmund Freud, describes running from a violent quarrel between his parents into the street, where a barrel organ was grinding out Ach, du lieber Augustin. Tragedy and the banal, side by side: it is a fair description of half his slow movements.

At fifteen he entered the Vienna Conservatory, studying piano and composition, and sat in on Bruckner’s harmony lectures at the University. His friends were Hugo Wolf and the short-lived Hans Rott, whose symphony sounds so much like Mahler’s own that Mahler later called Rott the founder of the new symphony, as he understood it. The cantata Das klagende Lied, completed in 1880, failed to win the Beethoven Prize in 1881. He had already begun the career that would pay for everything else: conducting.
